stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between $t$ and $L$?
stimulus:
A field technician checks a seismograph station and records $L$, the length, in meters, of recording paper remaining on the drum $t$ hours after a new roll is loaded. The table shows four of the readings.

Recording Paper Remaining on the Drum
Time since loading, t (hours) | 0 | 4 | 6 | 7
Paper remaining, L (meters) | 96 | 64 | 48 | 40
explanation: As $t$ increases, $L$ goes down, so the relationship is decreasing. The time readings are not evenly spaced (gaps of 4, 2 and 1 hours), so you have to compare each change in $L$ with the change in $t$. From 0 to 4 hours, $L$ drops 32 m in 4 h, which is 8 m per hour. From 4 to 6 hours, it drops 16 m in 2 h, which is 8 m per hour. From 6 to 7 hours, it drops 8 m in 1 h, which is 8 m per hour. The rate is a constant $-8$ meters per hour, so $L = 96 - 8t$. The relationship is decreasing linear.

B.why: You took the differences between neighbouring columns (−32, −16, −8), saw each one was half the one before, and decided the table shrinks by a constant factor. Those differences halve only because the time gaps halve (4, 2, 1 hours). Per hour, the drop is always 8 m. The ratios of $L$ itself (64/96, 48/64, 40/48) are not constant, so this is not exponential.

C.why: You found the constant rate of 8 meters per hour but tracked the paper used up (0, 32, 48, 56) instead of the paper remaining. The question asks about $L$, the paper remaining, and that goes down as $t$ increases.

D.why: You made two mistakes. You followed the paper used instead of the paper remaining, which flips the direction. You also treated the halving differences (32, 16, 8) as a constant multiplier, which changes the type. The paper remaining goes down by a constant 8 m per hour.

subtype_name: Linear vs exponential, increasing vs decreasing

stem: Which of the following statements is true?
stimulus: On day 0, the snow depth was 200 centimeters at weather Station P and 160 centimeters at weather Station Q. During a warm spell, Station P's snow depth decreased each day by an amount equal to 10% of its day 0 depth. Station Q's snow depth decreased each day by 15% of its depth at the end of the previous day. Depths are recorded at the end of each day.
choices: The depth at Station Q never exceeds the depth at Station P.
The depth at Station Q first exceeds Station P's at the end of day 7.
The depth at Station Q first exceeds Station P's at the end of day 8.
The depth at Station Q first exceeds Station P's at the end of day 10.
explanation: Station P loses 10% of a fixed amount, so it loses the same 20 cm every day. That makes it linear: $P(d) = 200 - 20d$. Station Q loses 15% of whatever depth it has, so it is exponential: $Q(d) = 160(0.85)^d$. A linear decrease reaches zero, but an exponential decrease never does, so Q has to pass P at some point. Check the end-of-day values. Day 7: $P = 60$ and $Q = 160(0.85)^7 \approx 51.3$, so P is still greater. Day 8: $P = 40$ and $Q = 160(0.85)^8 \approx 43.6$, so Q is greater. The depth at Q first exceeds the depth at P at the end of day 8.

A.why: You treated Station P's 10% as a percent of its current depth, so you modelled it as $200(0.9)^d$. Since 10% is a smaller loss than 15%, and P also starts higher, P would then stay ahead forever. In fact P loses 10% of its day 0 depth, a fixed 20 cm per day. That is linear, and Q overtakes it. You may also have judged only the first few days, when P is clearly ahead.

B.why: You set the two models equal, or found their intersection in Desmos, and got $d \approx 7.7$. Then you rounded down. At the end of day 7, P is still at 60 cm and Q is only about 51.3 cm. Depths are recorded at the end of each day, so the first recorded day with Q ahead is day 8.

D.why: You found when Station P's snow is completely gone ($200 \div 20 = 10$ days) and assumed Q could only pass P then. Q only has to be greater than P, not greater than zero, and that happens two days earlier, at the end of day 8, when P has 40 cm and Q has about 43.6 cm.
